## The problem

Our team of twelve engineers has drifted toward long-lived feature branches, some surviving two to three weeks before merging. Integration has become a recurring source of pain rather than a routine event. Merge conflicts multiply the longer a branch survives, code review happens against stale diffs that no longer reflect main, and QA often discovers integration bugs only after a branch lands, when the original author has moved on to something else. We are effectively deferring the hardest part of collaborative development — integration — until it is most expensive to fix. Concretely:

- Three of our last five production incidents traced back to merge conflicts resolved incorrectly under time pressure.
- Average branch lifetime has grown from roughly four days to eleven over the past two quarters, and is still climbing.

## The proposal

I propose we move to trunk-based development: engineers commit small, frequent changes directly to main, or via branches merged within a day, with incomplete work hidden behind feature flags rather than isolated on long branches. To make this work, we need three things in place before we flip the switch:

- A CI pipeline that runs the full test suite on every commit to main with fast feedback, ideally under ten minutes.
- Feature flag infrastructure so unfinished or risky work can ship dark and be toggled off without blocking anyone else.
- A team norm of small, reviewable pull requests, ideally under 400 lines, merged within 24 hours of opening.

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is real: trunk-based development pushes instability directly into main, which every engineer depends on daily, whereas a broken feature branch today only affects its author. If our CI is too slow or too flaky to catch regressions before they land, we could turn eleven isolated problems into one shared one. Feature flags add their own tax too — stale flags accumulate as debt, and toggle logic can itself become a source of bugs. This transition is not free, and we should not sell it as such; it demands real upfront investment in CI reliability and flag hygiene before we commit the whole team.

The remaining risks are smaller: some engineers will need time adjusting to smaller, more frequent commits, which we can address with pairing and a two-week trial on a single service before a full rollout.

Given the direction our incident trend is heading, I believe the cost of continuing as we are now exceeds the cost of making this change. I would like a decision by the end of next week.
